claim: CARD8 detects HIV-1 infection by sensing the enzymatic activity of the HIV protease, resulting in CARD8-dependent inflammasome activation.
source: Our previous work demonstrated that CARD8 detects HIV-1 infection by sensing the enzymatic activity of the HIV protease, resulting in CARD8-dependent inflammasome activation (Kulsuptrakul et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work (Kulsuptrakul et al., 2023)

claim: CARD8 harbors a motif in its N-terminus that functions as a HIV protease substrate mimic.
source: CARD8 harbors a motif in its N-terminus that functions as a HIV protease substrate mimic, permitting innate immune recognition of HIV-1 protease activity, which when cleaved by HIV protease triggers CARD8 inflammasome activation.
evidence: Stated as established fact in the abstract

claim: Cell-to-cell transmission of HIV-1 between infected T cells and primary human monocyte-derived macrophages induces CARD8 inflammasome activation in a manner that is dependent on viral protease activity.
source: We observed that cell-to-cell transmission of HIV-1 between infected T cells and primary human monocyte-derived macrophages induces CARD8 inflammasome activation in a manner that is dependent on viral protease activity and largely independent of the NLRP3 inflammasome.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript

claim: Cell-to-cell transmission of HIV-1 between infected T cells and primary human monocyte-derived macrophages induces CARD8 inflammasome activation in a manner that is largely independent of the NLRP3 inflammasome.
source: We observed that cell-to-cell transmission of HIV-1 between infected T cells and primary human monocyte-derived macrophages induces CARD8 inflammasome activation in a manner that is dependent on viral protease activity and largely independent of the NLRP3 inflammasome.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript

claim: Natural variation in HIV protease affects the cleavage of the viral Gag-Pol polyprotein.
source: Our results extend the role of incoming HIVPR on CARD8-dependent inflammasome activation of inflammasome responses as a function of cell type, mode of transmission, and virus evolution in response to antiviral therapy.
evidence: Inferred from the context of protease inhibitor resistance mutations and their effects

claim: Natural variation in HIV protease likely impacts innate sensing and inflammation.
source: We identified mutant HIV-1 proteases that differentially cleave and activate CARD8 compared to wildtype HIV-1, thus indicating that natural variation in HIV protease affects not only the cleavage of the viral Gag-Pol polyprotein but also likely impacts innate sensing and inflammation.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing differential CARD8 cleavage by PI-R mutants

claim: HIV-1 disease progression is characterized by chronic inflammation, immune activation, CD4+ T cell depletion and eventual destruction of the immune system and susceptibility to opportunistic infections.
source: HIV-1 disease progression is characterized by chronic inflammation, immune activation, CD4+ T cell depletion and eventual destruction of the immune system and susceptibility to opportunistic infections.
evidence: Established scientific knowledge about HIV-1 pathogenesis

claim: The primary cellular targets of HIV-1 are activated CD4+ T helper cells, specialized CD4+ T cell subtypes such as Th17 cells, central memory cells, and macrophages.
source: The primary cellular targets of HIV-1 are activated CD4+ T helper cells, specialized CD4+ T cell subtypes such as Th17 cells (Brenchley et al., 2008; Gosselin et al., 2010; Rodriguez-Garcia et al., 2014), central memory cells (Chun et al., 1997; Chun et al., 1995), and macrophages (Collman et al., 1990; Collman et al., 1989).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior research

claim: Chronic immune activation is primarily caused by rapid depletion of mucosal Th17 cells responsible for maintaining gut epithelial barrier integrity.
source: Chronic immune activation is primarily caused by rapid depletion of mucosal Th17 cells responsible for maintaining gut epithelial barrier integrity (Brenchley et al., 2008; Brenchley et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: Inflammasome activation ultimately results in activation of pro-inflammatory caspases including caspase 1 (CASP1).
source: Inflammasome activation ultimately results in activation of pro-inflammatory caspases including caspase 1 (CASP1).
evidence: Established knowledge about inflammasome biology

claim: Active CASP1 processes inflammatory cytokines and activates the pore-forming protein gasdermin D (GSDMD).
source: Active CASP1 processes inflammatory cytokines and activates the pore-forming protein gasdermin D (GSDMD), which forms small pores in the plasma membrane and initiates a lytic form of cell death known as pyroptosis and the release of mature inflammatory cytokines interleukin (IL)-1β and IL-18 (Broz and Dixit, 2016; Fink and Cookson, 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: GSDMD forms small pores in the plasma membrane and initiates a lytic form of cell death known as pyroptosis.
source: Active CASP1 processes inflammatory cytokines and activates the pore-forming protein gasdermin D (GSDMD), which forms small pores in the plasma membrane and initiates a lytic form of cell death known as pyroptosis and the release of mature inflammatory cytokines interleukin (IL)-1β and IL-18 (Broz and Dixit, 2016; Fink and Cookson, 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: The inflammasome-forming sensor CARD8 senses HIV-1 infection through the detection of HIV-1 protease (HIVPR) activity.
source: In prior work, we and others showed that the inflammasome-forming sensor CARD8 senses HIV-1 infection through the detection of HIV-1 protease (HIVPR) activity (Clark et al., 2023; Kulsuptrakul et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research including authors' own work

claim: Active HIVPR is released into the host cell, which is sensed by CARD8 via HIVPR cleavage of its N-terminus and subsequent inflammasome activation.
source: While the canonical function of HIVPR is to cleave viral polyproteins during virion maturation, active HIVPR is also released into the host cell, which is sensed by CARD8 via HIVPR cleavage of its N-terminus and subsequent inflammasome activation.
evidence: Supported by prior research cited in the manuscript

claim: The CARD8 N-terminus functions as a 'molecular tripwire' to recognize the enzymatic activity of HIVPR and other viral proteases.
source: In this way, the CARD8 N-terminus functions as a 'molecular tripwire' to recognize the enzymatic activity of HIVPR and other viral proteases (Castro and Daugherty, 2023; Nadkarni et al., 2022; Tsu et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: HIVPR cleavage of CARD8 occurs rapidly after infection such that HIVPR inhibitors and fusion inhibitors, but not reverse transcriptase (RT) inhibitors can prevent CARD8 inflammasome activation.
source: Moreover, HIVPR cleavage of CARD8 occurs rapidly after infection such that HIVPR inhibitors and fusion inhibitors, but not reverse transcriptase (RT) inhibitors can prevent CARD8 inflammasome activation, implying that CARD8 detects HIV-1 viral protease activity of virion-packaged or 'incoming' HIVPR upon virion fusion (Kulsuptrakul et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: CARD8 detects HIV-1 viral protease activity of virion-packaged or 'incoming' HIVPR upon virion fusion.
source: Moreover, HIVPR cleavage of CARD8 occurs rapidly after infection such that HIVPR inhibitors and fusion inhibitors, but not reverse transcriptase (RT) inhibitors can prevent CARD8 inflammasome activation, implying that CARD8 detects HIV-1 viral protease activity of virion-packaged or 'incoming' HIVPR upon virion fusion (Kulsuptrakul et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2021).
evidence: Inferred from experimental data cited in prior research

claim: CARD8 inflammasome activation in resting CD4+ T cells results in pyroptosis but not the release of pro-inflammatory cytokines IL-1β or IL-18.
source: Interestingly, CARD8 inflammasome activation in resting CD4+ T cells results in pyroptosis but not the release of pro-inflammatory cytokines IL-1β or IL-18 (Wang et al., 2024), suggesting that CARD8 inflammasome activation in T cells does not directly contribute to chronic inflammation.
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research

claim: CARD8 inflammasome activation in T cells does not directly contribute to chronic inflammation.
source: Interestingly, CARD8 inflammasome activation in resting CD4+ T cells results in pyroptosis but not the release of pro-inflammatory cytokines IL-1β or IL-18 (Wang et al., 2024), suggesting that CARD8 inflammasome activation in T cells does not directly contribute to chronic inflammation.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that T cells do not release IL-1β or IL-18

claim: HIV-1 can be transmitted from one cell to another via two main mechanisms: 'cell-free' infection through binding of free HIV-1 virions to target cells, and cell-to-cell infection whereby infected cells directly transfer virus to an uninfected target cell via the formation of a transient viral synapse.
source: HIV-1 can be transmitted from one cell to another via two main mechanisms: 'cell-free' infection through binding of free HIV-1 virions to target cells, and cell-to-cell infection whereby infected cells directly transfer virus to an uninfected target cell via the formation of a transient viral synapse (Chen et al., 2007; Galloway et al., 2015; Iwami et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: Cell-to-cell transmission of HIV-1 has been reported between multiple HIV-1 target cell types including between active and resting CD4+ T cells and between CD4+ T cells and macrophages.
source: Cell-to-cell transmission of HIV-1 has been reported between multiple HIV-1 target cell types including between active and resting CD4+ T cells (Agosto et al., 2018; Martin et al., 2010) and between CD4+ T cells and macrophages (Baxter et al., 2014; Dupont and Sattentau, 2020; Lopez et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: Cell-to-cell transmission delivers a large influx of virus to target cells, resulting in a high multiplicity of infection (MOI).
source: Cell-to-cell transmission delivers a large influx of virus to target cells, resulting in a high multiplicity of infection (MOI) (Agosto et al., 2015; Del Portillo et al., 2011; Duncan et al., 2013; Russell et al., 2013), which has been proposed to enhance viral fitness by overwhelming host restriction factors including Tetherin/BST-2 (Jolly et al., 2010; Zhong et al., 2013), SAMHD1 (Xie et al., 2019), and TRIM5α (Richardson et al., 2008), and evading adaptive immune responses including broadly neutralizing antibodies (Abela et al., 2012; Dufloo et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: Cell-to-cell transmission has been proposed to enhance viral fitness by overwhelming host restriction factors including Tetherin/BST-2, SAMHD1, and TRIM5α.
source: Cell-to-cell transmission delivers a large influx of virus to target cells, resulting in a high multiplicity of infection (MOI) (Agosto et al., 2015; Del Portillo et al., 2011; Duncan et al., 2013; Russell et al., 2013), which has been proposed to enhance viral fitness by overwhelming host restriction factors including Tetherin/BST-2 (Jolly et al., 2010; Zhong et al., 2013), SAMHD1 (Xie et al., 2019), and TRIM5α (Richardson et al., 2008), and evading adaptive immune responses including broadly neutralizing antibodies (Abela et al., 2012; Dufloo et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: Cell-to-cell transmission has been proposed to enhance viral fitness by evading adaptive immune responses including broadly neutralizing antibodies.
source: Cell-to-cell transmission delivers a large influx of virus to target cells, resulting in a high multiplicity of infection (MOI) (Agosto et al., 2015; Del Portillo et al., 2011; Duncan et al., 2013; Russell et al., 2013), which has been proposed to enhance viral fitness by overwhelming host restriction factors including Tetherin/BST-2 (Jolly et al., 2010; Zhong et al., 2013), SAMHD1 (Xie et al., 2019), and TRIM5α (Richardson et al., 2008), and evading adaptive immune responses including broadly neutralizing antibodies (Abela et al., 2012; Dufloo et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: SUPT1 cells do not have a functional CARD8 inflammasome pathway.
source: We opted for SUPT1 cells as the viral producer cell line because they are permissive to HIV-1 infection, and unlike THP-1 cells, SUPT1 cells do not respond to a known CARD8 inflammasome activator, ValboroPro (VbP), as assayed by both IL-1β secretion and cell death, indicating that SUPT1 cells do not have a functional CARD8 inflammasome pathway (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A

claim: Coculture of THP-1 cells with HIV-1LAI-infected SUPT1 cells but not mock-infected SUPT1 cells results in robust inflammasome activation as indicated by IL-1β secretion.
source: We found that coculture of THP-1 cells with HIV-1LAI-infected SUPT1 cells (Figure 1B) but not mock-infected SUPT1 cells results in robust inflammasome activation as indicated by IL-1β secretion, suggesting that our coculture system, which lacks DEAE-dextran, can induce HIV-dependent inflammasome activation via cell-to-cell infection (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1B and 1C

claim: HIV-1LAI-infected SUPT1 cells cocultured with THP-1 cells in a transwell system (preventing cell-to-cell contact) did not lead to detectable IL-1β secretion.
source: Despite equivalent amounts of infectious virus in both conditions, we observed that HIV-1LAI-infected SUPT1 cells (upper chamber) cocultured with THP-1 cells (lower chamber) did not lead to detectable IL-1β secretion (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C

claim: The SUPT1:THP-1 coculture system can trigger HIV-dependent inflammasome activation in a manner dependent on cell-to-cell contact.
source: These data suggest that our SUPT1:THP-1 coculture system can trigger HIV-dependent inflammasome activation in a manner dependent on cell-to-cell contact.
evidence: Inferred from the transwell experiment showing no IL-1β secretion without cell-to-cell contact

claim: HIV-1LAI-infected SUPT1 cells cocultured with WT but not CARD8 KO THP-1 cells resulted in a significant increase in IL-1β.
source: HIV-1LAI-infected SUPT1 cells cocultured with WT but not CARD8 KO THP-1 cells resulted in a significant increase in IL-1β (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A

claim: CARD8 is the primary sensor that drives inflammasome activation in HIV-1 cell-to-cell transmission to THP-1 cells.
source: These results suggest that CARD8 is the primary sensor that drives inflammasome activation in HIV-1 cell-to-cell transmission to THP-1 cells.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that CARD8 KO THP-1 cells do not produce IL-1β upon HIV-1 coculture

claim: The NLRP3 inflammasome has previously been implicated in HIV-dependent inflammasome activation.
source: Since the NLRP3 inflammasome has previously been implicated in HIV-dependent inflammasome activation (Bandera et al., 2018; Chivero et al., 2017; Hernandez et al., 2014; Leal et al., 2020; Mamik et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2021), we also assessed the effects of the NLRP3 inflammasome-specific inhibitor MCC950 (Coll et al., 2015; Primiano et al., 2016) on inflammasome activation in our coculture system.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: Treatment with MCC950 or the caspase 1 (CASP1) inhibitor VX765 were sufficient to abrogate inflammasome activation induced by the ionophore nigericin.
source: Treatment with MCC950 or the caspase 1 (CASP1) inhibitor VX765 (Wannamaker et al., 2007) were sufficient to abrogate inflammasome activation induced by the ionophore nigericin, a well-characterized NLRP3 agonist (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A

claim: In the HIV-1 coculture system, MCC950 treatment had only a modest effect on inflammasome activation while VX765 and the HIVPR inhibitor lopinavir (LPV) completely abrogated IL-1β secretion.
source: However, in the HIV-1 coculture system, MCC950 treatment had only a modest effect on inflammasome activation while VX765 and the HIVPR inhibitor lopinavir (LPV), which prevents CARD8 cleavage by HIV-1PR (Kulsuptrakul et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2021), completely abrogated IL-1β secretion (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B

claim: HIV-dependent inflammasome activation via cell-to-cell transmission is CARD8-dependent and largely NLRP3-independent.
source: Taken together, these findings indicate that HIV-dependent inflammasome activation via cell-to-cell transmission is CARD8-dependent and largely NLRP3-independent.
evidence: Inferred from the differential effects of CARD8 KO and MCC950 treatment on IL-1β secretion

claim: MDMs cocultured with HIV-1NL4.3-BaL-infected SUPT1 cells but not with mock- or HIV-1LAI-infected SUPT1-CCR5 cells showed inflammasome activation as measured by IL-1β secretion.
source: We observed inflammasome activation, as measured by IL-1β secretion, in MDMs cocultured with HIV-1NL4.3-BaL-infected SUPT1 cells but not in MDMs cocultured with mock- or HIV-1LAI-infected SUPT1-CCR5 cells (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A

claim: HIV-dependent inflammasome activation can occur in MDMs during cell-to-cell infection in a manner dependent on viral entry.
source: This demonstrates that HIV-dependent inflammasome activation can occur in MDMs during cell-to-cell infection in a manner dependent on viral entry.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that only CCR5-tropic HIV-1NL4.3-BaL, which can enter macrophages, induced IL-1β secretion

claim: IL-1β secretion in MDM cocultures was abrogated by treatment with lopinavir, an HIV-1 protease inhibitor, and VX765, a CASP1 inhibitor.
source: We observed that IL-1β secretion was abrogated by treatment with lopinavir, an HIV-1 protease inhibitor, and VX765, a CASP1 inhibitor, indicating that inflammasome activation in MDM cocultures is dependent on HIVPR and CASP1, respectively (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A

claim: Inflammasome activation in MDM cocultures is dependent on HIVPR and CASP1.
source: We observed that IL-1β secretion was abrogated by treatment with lopinavir, an HIV-1 protease inhibitor, and VX765, a CASP1 inhibitor, indicating that inflammasome activation in MDM cocultures is dependent on HIVPR and CASP1, respectively (Figure 3A).
evidence: Inferred from the observation that inhibitors of HIVPR and CASP1 block IL-1β secretion

claim: HIV-dependent inflammasome activation was observed in the presence of NVP (an RT inhibitor) that was added at the time of coculture, indicating that incoming HIVPR is sufficient to elicit an inflammasome response.
source: Indeed, we observed HIV-dependent inflammasome activation in the presence of NVP that was added at the time of coculture, indicating that incoming HIVPR is sufficient to elicit an inflammasome response (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A

claim: MDM cocultures treated with MCC950, an inhibitor of the NLRP3 inflammasome, had no effect on IL-1β secretion.
source: Lastly, MDM cocultures treated with MCC950, an inhibitor of the NLRP3 inflammasome, had no effect on IL-1β secretion (Figure 3A), and we observed similar inflammasome activation results regardless of whether the MDMs were primed with TLR1/2 agonist Pam3CSK4 versus TLR4 agonist lipopolysaccharide (LPS) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A

claim: Cell-to-cell contact of infected cells with primary monocyte-derived macrophages can elicit an inflammasome response in a manner that is dependent on viral entry, CASP1, and incoming HIVPR, and independent from NLRP3.
source: Thus, cell-to-cell contact of infected cells with primary monocyte-derived macrophages can elicit an inflammasome response in a manner that is dependent on viral entry, CASP1, and incoming HIVPR, and independent from NLRP3.
evidence: Inferred from the combined results of inhibitor treatments and viral tropism experiments

claim: Inflammasome activation as determined by IL-1β secretion was detected by 24 hours post coculture in all donors and persisted at a similar level at 48 and 72 hours post coculture.
source: We observed inflammasome activation as determined by IL-1β secretion by 24 hours post coculture in all donors that persisted at a similar level at 48 and 72 hours post coculture (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B

claim: Adding NVP had no effect on IL-1β secretion in HIV-1-infected MDM cocultures.
source: Moreover, adding NVP had no effect on IL-1β secretion in HIV-1-infected MDM cocultures (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B

claim: In the context of cell-to-cell transmission, CARD8 is likely the inflammasome-forming sensor that detects HIV-1 infection via incoming HIVPR activity in primary monocyte-derived macrophages.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that in the context of cell-to-cell transmission, CARD8 is likely the inflammasome-forming sensor that detects HIV-1 infection via incoming HIVPR activity in primary monocyte-derived macrophages.
evidence: Inferred from the combined results showing dependence on HIVPR but not RT, and independence from NLRP3

claim: A marked reduction of the full-length and FIIND-processed CARD8 protein was observed in CARD8 KO MDMs relative to the AAVS1 KO control in all five donors.
source: To verify KO efficiency, we immunoblotted with an antibody that detects the CARD8 C-terminus in CARD8 KO MDMs relative to the AAVS1 KO control and observed a marked reduction of the full-length and FIIND-processed CARD8 protein in all five donors (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C

claim: Significant reduction in inflammasome activation was observed in CARD8 KO cocultures relative to the AAVS1 KO control in all five donors.
source: In all five donors, we observed significant reduction in inflammasome activation in CARD8 KO cocultures relative to the AAVS1 KO control (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D

claim: No difference in inflammasome activation was observed when coculturing infected SUPT1 cells with AAVS1 KO vs NLRP3 KO MDMs.
source: Consistent with our findings with SUPT1:THP-1 coculture, we observed no difference in inflammasome activation when coculturing infected SUPT1 cells with AAVS1 KO vs NLRP3 KO MDMs, suggesting that the inflammasome activation was also largely NLRP3-independent (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D

claim: CARD8 is required for inflammasome activation in MDMs during HIV-1 cell-to cell transmission.
source: Taken together, these data demonstrate that CARD8 is required for inflammasome activation in MDMs during HIV-1 cell-to cell transmission.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that CARD8 KO MDMs do not produce IL-1β upon HIV-1 coculture

claim: Inflammasome activation was observed when coculturing with HIV-infected T cells but not mock-infected T cells or cocultures treated with LPV or VX765.
source: We assessed inflammasome activation via IL-1β secretion 72 hours post coculture and observed inflammasome activation when coculturing with HIV-infected T cells but not mock-infected T cells or cocultures treated with LPV or VX765, demonstrating that inflammasome activation is driven by HIVPR and CASP1 (Figure 4A) and consistent with our findings using the SUPT1:MDM coculture (Figure 3).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A

claim: Inflammasome activation in the CD4:MDM coculture is driven by HIVPR and CASP1.
source: We assessed inflammasome activation via IL-1β secretion 72 hours post coculture and observed inflammasome activation when coculturing with HIV-infected T cells but not mock-infected T cells or cocultures treated with LPV or VX765, demonstrating that inflammasome activation is driven by HIVPR and CASP1 (Figure 4A) and consistent with our findings using the SUPT1:MDM coculture (Figure 3).
evidence: Inferred from the observation that inhibitors of HIVPR and CASP1 block IL-1β secretion

claim: Inflammasome activation persisted in NVP-treated cocultures, suggesting that incoming protease is also important for inflammasome activation in the context of cell-to-cell transmission of HIV-1 from primary CD4+ T cells to primary MDMs.
source: We also observed that inflammasome activation persisted in NVP-treated cocultures, suggesting that incoming protease is also important for inflammasome activation in the context of cell-to-cell transmission of HIV-1 from primary CD4+ T cells to primary MDMs (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A

claim: Elevated levels of IL-1β were detected by 24 hours post coculture in the CD4:MDM coculture, which was strictly dependent on the enzymatic activity of the viral protease as LPV treatment completely inhibited IL-1β secretion.
source: Similar to the SUPT1:MDM time course (Figure 3B), we were able to detect elevated levels of IL-1β by 24 hours post coculture, which was again strictly dependent on the enzymatic activity of the viral protease as LPV treatment completely inhibited IL-1β secretion (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B

claim: A significant decrease in inflammasome activation was detected when infected T cells were cocultured with CARD8 KO versus AAVS1 KO MDMs.
source: We detected a significant decrease in inflammasome activation when infected T cells were cocultured with CARD8 KO versus AAVS1 KO MDMs (Figure 4D), indicating that CARD8 is required for inflammasome activation in MDMs during HIV-1 transmission from primary CD4+ T cells to MDMs.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D

claim: CARD8 is required for inflammasome activation in MDMs during HIV-1 transmission from primary CD4+ T cells to MDMs.
source: We detected a significant decrease in inflammasome activation when infected T cells were cocultured with CARD8 KO versus AAVS1 KO MDMs (Figure 4D), indicating that CARD8 is required for inflammasome activation in MDMs during HIV-1 transmission from primary CD4+ T cells to MDMs.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that CARD8 KO MDMs do not produce IL-1β upon HIV-1 coculture with primary CD4+ T cells

claim: CARD8 plays a pivotal role in sensing and responding to HIV-1 cell-to-cell infection between primary CD4 T cells and macrophages.
source: Taken together, our data indicate that CARD8 plays a pivotal role in sensing and responding to HIV-1 cell-to-cell infection between primary CD4 T cells and macrophages.
evidence: Inferred from the combined results showing CARD8 dependence in primary cell cocultures

claim: A PI-R clone (PI-R1) exhibited similar efficiency at cleaving CARD8 to HIV-1LAI.
source: By quantifying the 33 kDa CARD8 cleavage product with each HIV-1 provirus, we identified a PI-R clone that exhibited similar efficiency at cleaving CARD8 to HIV-1LAI (i.e., PI-R1), PI-R clones that were markedly less efficient at cleaving CARD8 than HIV-1LAI (i.e., PI-R2, PI-R3, PI-R5, PI-R9, and PI-R10) and two PI-R clones, PI-R12 and PI-R13, that were more efficient at cleaving CARD8 than HIV-1LAI (Figure 5A, top, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A

claim: PI-R clones (PI-R2, PI-R3, PI-R5, PI-R9, and PI-R10) were markedly less efficient at cleaving CARD8 than HIV-1LAI.
source: By quantifying the 33 kDa CARD8 cleavage product with each HIV-1 provirus, we identified a PI-R clone that exhibited similar efficiency at cleaving CARD8 to HIV-1LAI (i.e., PI-R1), PI-R clones that were markedly less efficient at cleaving CARD8 than HIV-1LAI (i.e., PI-R2, PI-R3, PI-R5, PI-R9, and PI-R10) and two PI-R clones, PI-R12 and PI-R13, that were more efficient at cleaving CARD8 than HIV-1LAI (Figure 5A, top, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A

claim: Two PI-R clones, PI-R12 and PI-R13, were more efficient at cleaving CARD8 than HIV-1LAI.
source: By quantifying the 33 kDa CARD8 cleavage product with each HIV-1 provirus, we identified a PI-R clone that exhibited similar efficiency at cleaving CARD8 to HIV-1LAI (i.e., PI-R1), PI-R clones that were markedly less efficient at cleaving CARD8 than HIV-1LAI (i.e., PI-R2, PI-R3, PI-R5, PI-R9, and PI-R10) and two PI-R clones, PI-R12 and PI-R13, that were more efficient at cleaving CARD8 than HIV-1LAI (Figure 5A, top, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A

claim: All PI-R proviruses had similar levels of HIVPR activity for HIVgagpol polyprotein processing from p55gag to p24gag as indicated by the ratio of p24gag/p55gag.
source: Of note, all PI-R proviruses had similar levels of HIVPR activity for HIVgagpol polyprotein processing from p55gag to p24gag as indicated by the ratio of p24gag/p55gag quantified from the anti-p24gag immunoblot (Figure 5A, middle).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A

claim: Naturally occurring HIV-1 protease mutations can influence host targets like CARD8.
source: These results indicate that naturally occurring HIV-1 protease mutations can influence host targets like CARD8.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that PI-R clones differentially cleave CARD8

claim: PI-R2 and PI-R9, which exhibited less CARD8 cleavage than HIV-1LAI, also induced lower IL-1β levels than HIV-1LAI.
source: Consistent with the observed differences in CARD8 cleavage by PI-R clones (Figure 5A), we found that PI-R2 and PI-R9, which exhibited less CARD8 cleavage than HIV-1LAI, also induced lower IL-1β levels than HIV-1LAI (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B

claim: PI-R12 and PI-R13, which demonstrated enhanced CARD8 cleavage, elicited higher IL-1β levels than HIV-1LAI.
source: Similarly, PI-R12 and PI-R13, which demonstrated enhanced CARD8 cleavage, elicited higher IL-1β levels than HIV-1LAI (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B

claim: Cell-to-cell transmission of PI-R2 and PI-R9 resulted in lower IL-1β levels while PI-R12 and PI-R13 resulted in higher IL-1β levels compared to HIV-1LAI.
source: In these HEK293T:THP-1 cocultures, we observed that cell-to-cell transmission of PI-R2 and PI-R9 resulted in lower IL-1β levels while PI-R12 and PI-R13 resulted in higher IL-1β levels compared to HIV-1LAI, respectively (Figure 5C), consistent with our findings from CARD8 cleavage (Figure 5A) and reconstituted inflammasome assays (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C

claim: HIV-dependent inflammasome activation is under genetic control of the viral protease in a manner that can be increased or decreased with naturally occurring mutations induced by drug resistance.
source: Our findings suggest that HIV-dependent inflammasome activation is under genetic control of the viral protease in a manner that can be increased or decreased with naturally occurring mutations induced by drug resistance.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that PI-R clones with different protease mutations differentially activate CARD8

claim: Cell-to-cell transmission of HIV-1 from T cells to myeloid cells in both immortalized and primary cell coculture models of infection yields CARD8-dependent inflammasome activation via incoming HIVPR.
source: We demonstrate that cell-to-cell transmission of HIV-1 from T cells to myeloid cells in both immortalized and primary cell coculture models of infection yields CARD8-dependent inflammasome activation via incoming HIVPR.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented throughout the manuscript

claim: This inflammasome activation occurs in a largely NLRP3-independent manner.
source: This inflammasome activation occurs in a largely NLRP3-independent manner.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing minimal effect of MCC950 and no difference between AAVS1 KO and NLRP3 KO MDMs

claim: HIVPR mutants selected for their resistance to different protease inhibitors also affect their ability to cleave host proteins including the inflammasome-forming sensor CARD8.
source: Thus, HIVPR mutants selected for their resistance to different protease inhibitors also affect their ability to cleave host proteins including the inflammasome-forming sensor CARD8.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing differential CARD8 cleavage by PI-R clones

claim: Both the NLRP3 and IFI16 inflammasomes had been implicated as innate sensors of HIV-1 infection and drivers of CD4+ T cell depletion.
source: Previously, both the NLRP3 and IFI16 inflammasomes had been implicated as innate sensors of HIV-1 infection and drivers of CD4+ T cell depletion using blood and lymphoid-derived CD4+ T cells, respectively, and cell-to-cell transmission was reported to be crucial for IFI16 sensing of abortive HIV transcripts (Doitsh et al., 2014; Galloway et al., 2015; Monroe et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: Cell-to-cell transmission was reported to be crucial for IFI16 sensing of abortive HIV transcripts.
source: Previously, both the NLRP3 and IFI16 inflammasomes had been implicated as innate sensors of HIV-1 infection and drivers of CD4+ T cell depletion using blood and lymphoid-derived CD4+ T cells, respectively, and cell-to-cell transmission was reported to be crucial for IFI16 sensing of abortive HIV transcripts (Doitsh et al., 2014; Galloway et al., 2015; Monroe et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: CARD8 is expressed and functional in naïve and memory CD4+ and CD8+ T cells.
source: Indeed, CARD8, which is expressed and functional in naïve and memory CD4+ and CD8+ T cells (Linder et al., 2020), was recently shown to be required for pyroptosis in primary human blood- and lymphoid-derived CD4+ T cells and humanized mouse models (Wang et al., 2024), implicating CARD8 as a major driver of CD4+ T cell depletion during HIV-1 infection.
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research

claim: CARD8 was recently shown to be required for pyroptosis in primary human blood- and lymphoid-derived CD4+ T cells and humanized mouse models.
source: Indeed, CARD8, which is expressed and functional in naïve and memory CD4+ and CD8+ T cells (Linder et al., 2020), was recently shown to be required for pyroptosis in primary human blood- and lymphoid-derived CD4+ T cells and humanized mouse models (Wang et al., 2024), implicating CARD8 as a major driver of CD4+ T cell depletion during HIV-1 infection.
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research

claim: CARD8 is a major driver of CD4+ T cell depletion during HIV-1 infection.
source: Indeed, CARD8, which is expressed and functional in naïve and memory CD4+ and CD8+ T cells (Linder et al., 2020), was recently shown to be required for pyroptosis in primary human blood- and lymphoid-derived CD4+ T cells and humanized mouse models (Wang et al., 2024), implicating CARD8 as a major driver of CD4+ T cell depletion during HIV-1 infection.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that CARD8 is required for pyroptosis in CD4+ T cells

claim: CARD8 is also the primary innate sensor during HIV-1 infection in myeloid cell types during cell-to-cell transmission.
source: In this study and our prior work (Kulsuptrakul et al., 2023), we demonstrate that CARD8 is also the primary innate sensor during HIV-1 infection in myeloid cell types during cell-to-cell transmission.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript and prior work

claim: The degree of inflammation is a better predictor of disease progression in untreated individuals than viral load.
source: As the degree of inflammation is a better predictor of disease progression in untreated individuals than viral load (Deeks et al., 2004; Giorgi et al., 1999), we speculate that differential CARD8 inflammasome activation could influence disease progression for PLWH harboring HIVPR resistance mutations that cleave CARD8 more or less efficiently.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: Differential CARD8 inflammasome activation could influence disease progression for PLWH harboring HIVPR resistance mutations that cleave CARD8 more or less efficiently.
source: As the degree of inflammation is a better predictor of disease progression in untreated individuals than viral load (Deeks et al., 2004; Giorgi et al., 1999), we speculate that differential CARD8 inflammasome activation could influence disease progression for PLWH harboring HIVPR resistance mutations that cleave CARD8 more or less efficiently.
evidence: Speculative reasoning based on the observation that PI-R clones differentially activate CARD8 and the known relationship between inflammation and disease progression

claim: Host targets of viral proteases like CARD8 may influence the selection of viral variants during treatment with antiviral protease inhibitor monotherapies.
source: More broadly, we suggest that host targets of viral proteases like CARD8 may influence the selection of viral variants during treatment with antiviral protease inhibitor monotherapies.
evidence: Speculative reasoning based on the observation that PI-R clones differentially activate CARD8

claim: HIV-dependent CARD8 inflammasome activation during cell-free infection requires a cationic polymer like DEAE-dextran to facilitate efficient viral infection.
source: In this study, we found that HIV-dependent CARD8 inflammasome activation during cell-free infection requires a cationic polymer like DEAE-dextran to facilitate efficient viral infection (see Appendix 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in Appendix 1

claim: DEAE-dextran during cell-free infection may increase the total viral dose that enters cells.
source: Despite being infected with the same amount of virus and exhibiting similar percent infection 24 hours post-infection, as measured by intracellular p24gag, with and without DEAE-dextran, we hypothesize that DEAE-dextran during cell-free infection may increase the total viral dose that enters cells.
evidence: Speculative reasoning to explain the requirement for DEAE-dextran

claim: A considerable influx of incoming HIVPR may be necessary to induce CARD8 inflammasome activation.
source: We speculate that a considerable influx of incoming HIVPR may be necessary to induce CARD8 inflammasome activation.
evidence: Speculative reasoning based on the observation that DEAE-dextran is required for cell-free infection

claim: DEAE-dextran can trigger inflammasome activation in some THP-1 cell lines.
source: We also observed that DEAE-dextran can trigger inflammasome activation in some THP-1 cell lines (see Appendix 1), prompting us to assay for inflammasome activation upon HIV-1 cell-to-cell transmission with target cells at a 1:1 ratio in the absence of cationic polymer.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in Appendix 1

claim: Inflammasome activation following cell-to-cell transmission of HIV-1 could be detected by 24 hours.
source: We found that inflammasome activation following cell-to-cell transmission of HIV-1 could be detected by 24 hours (Figure 3B), which is delayed relative to our detection of CARD8 inflammasome activation 2 hours post cell-free HIV-1 infection in the presence of DEAE-dextran (Kulsuptrakul et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B

claim: IL-1β levels do not increase after plateauing 24 hours after establishing the coculture.
source: Similarly, we observed that IL-1β levels do not increase after plateauing 24 hours after establishing the coculture (Figures 3B and 4B), suggesting that secondary infection does not further amplify inflammasome activation.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3B and 4B

claim: Secondary infection does not further amplify inflammasome activation.
source: Similarly, we observed that IL-1β levels do not increase after plateauing 24 hours after establishing the coculture (Figures 3B and 4B), suggesting that secondary infection does not further amplify inflammasome activation.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that IL-1β levels plateau after 24 hours

claim: Under certain physiological conditions, cell-to-cell transmission can cause CARD8 inflammasome activation when there is an influx of active incoming HIVPR across the viral synapse.
source: We postulate that under certain physiological conditions, cell-to-cell transmission can cause CARD8 inflammasome activation when there is an influx of active incoming HIVPR across the viral synapse.
evidence: Speculative reasoning based on the experimental observations

claim: Both cell-free infection facilitated by cationic polymer and cell-to-cell transmission can achieve sufficient levels of active HIVPR influx to activate the CARD8 inflammasome.
source: Taken together, we speculate that both cell-free infection facilitated by cationic polymer and cell-to-cell transmission can achieve sufficient levels of active HIVPR influx to activate the CARD8 inflammasome.
evidence: Speculative reasoning based on the combined experimental observations

claim: Macrophages have been reported to be primarily infected through phagocytosis of infected CD4+ T cells or cell-to-cell transmission.
source: Macrophages have been reported to be primarily infected through phagocytosis of infected CD4+ T cells or cell-to-cell transmission (Dupont and Sattentau, 2020; Martínez-Méndez et al., 2017; Orenstein, 2000).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: Unlike CD4+ T cells, which are rapidly depleted by HIV-1 infection and do not release IL-1β or IL-18, primary macrophages release pro-inflammatory cytokines in response to HIVPR during cell-to-cell infection from infected primary CD4+ T cells and T cell lines.
source: We demonstrate that unlike CD4+ T cells, which are rapidly depleted by HIV-1 infection and do not release IL-1β or IL-18 (Linder et al., 2020), primary macrophages release pro-inflammatory cytokines in response to HIVPR during cell-to-cell infection from infected primary CD4+ T cells and T cell lines (Figures 3 and 4), thus representing a potential source of sustained IL-1β and subsequent chronic immune activation.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3 and 4 and citation to prior research

claim: Primary macrophages represent a potential source of sustained IL-1β and subsequent chronic immune activation.
source: We demonstrate that unlike CD4+ T cells, which are rapidly depleted by HIV-1 infection and do not release IL-1β or IL-18 (Linder et al., 2020), primary macrophages release pro-inflammatory cytokines in response to HIVPR during cell-to-cell infection from infected primary CD4+ T cells and T cell lines (Figures 3 and 4), thus representing a potential source of sustained IL-1β and subsequent chronic immune activation.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that macrophages release IL-1β in response to HIV-1

claim: HIV-dependent IL-1β release from macrophages may contribute to HIV-1 pathogenesis by activating nearby CD4+ T cells, rendering them susceptible to becoming infected with HIV-1, and thus indirectly promoting CD4+ T cell depletion.
source: In addition to promoting chronic immune activation, HIV-dependent IL-1β release from macrophages may also contribute to HIV-1 pathogenesis by activating nearby CD4+ T cells, rendering them susceptible to becoming infected with HIV-1, and thus indirectly promoting CD4+ T cell depletion.
evidence: Speculative reasoning about the potential consequences of IL-1β release from macrophages

claim: CARD8 inflammasome activation is driven by incoming HIVPR under conditions where multiple virions may enter cells.
source: Collectively with our prior work (Kulsuptrakul et al., 2023), our findings provide further evidence that CARD8 inflammasome activation is driven by incoming HIVPR under conditions where multiple virions may enter cells, and thus could be a potential driver of HIV-1 pathogenesis by promoting chronic immune activation.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript and prior work

claim: CARD8 inflammasome activation could be a potential driver of HIV-1 pathogenesis by promoting chronic immune activation.
source: Collectively with our prior work (Kulsuptrakul et al., 2023), our findings provide further evidence that CARD8 inflammasome activation is driven by incoming HIVPR under conditions where multiple virions may enter cells, and thus could be a potential driver of HIV-1 pathogenesis by promoting chronic immune activation.
evidence: Speculative reasoning based on the experimental observations

claim: HIV-1LAI protease cleaves CARD8 between phenylalanine (F) 59 and F60.
source: HIV-1LAI protease cleaves CARD8 between phenylalanine (F) 59 and F60 (Wang et al., 2021), resulting in an ~33 kDa product (Figure 5A, top).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research and experimental data shown in Figure 5A

claim: CARD8 inflammasome activation in the HEK293T:THP-1 coculture system is consistent with findings from CARD8 cleavage and reconstituted inflammasome assays.
source: In these HEK293T:THP-1 cocultures, we observed that cell-to-cell transmission of PI-R2 and PI-R9 resulted in lower IL-1β levels while PI-R12 and PI-R13 resulted in higher IL-1β levels compared to HIV-1LAI, respectively (Figure 5C), consistent with our findings from CARD8 cleavage (Figure 5A) and reconstituted inflammasome assays (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figures 5A, 5B, and 5C
